Enterprise adds codebase-level indexing, fine-tuned private models, and $39 in monthly AI Credits per user on top of everything in Business. It needs GitHub Enterprise Cloud as a prerequisite, which carries its own per-seat cost on top of the Copilot license.

# GitHub Copilot Impact Analysis: Prove ROI That Survives

*Written by: Mark Hull, Co-Founder and CEO, Exceeds AI | Last updated: September 11, 2026*

## How To Measure GitHub Copilot’s Impact

A defensible GitHub Copilot impact analysis follows a connected, seven-step sequence that moves from goals to financial outcomes.

1. Define the outcome before the tool. Decide what success looks like for your organization before touching the data.
2. Pick a comparison design. Choose a before/after or cohort design, and document why that design fits your environment.
3. Control for confounders. Account for project complexity, developer tenure, staffing changes, release seasonality, and concurrent tool changes.
4. Measure at four levels. Track adoption, developer productivity, engineering outcomes, and business value as distinct signal layers.
5. Watch for commit inflation. Flag rising commit and line counts that do not reflect durable engineering value.
6. Track AI-touched code over 30+ days. Capture the maintenance and incident story that point-in-time quality metrics miss.
7. Account for the full AI toolchain. Include Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, Windsurf, and other tools that sit alongside Copilot.

## What The Credible Evidence Actually Says

[The Peng et al. (2023) randomized controlled trial (arXiv:2302.06590) recruited developers to implement an HTTP server in JavaScript and found the Copilot group finished 55.8% faster](https://github.com/AvneeshSarwate/ai-econ-research/blob/main/summaries/peng-2023-github-copilot-productivity.md). The internal validity is strong for that bounded, greenfield task. The external validity is weak because the study measured one well-specified task and excluded quality, maintenance, debugging, architecture, and integration work. It is best read as a task-specif

### Which has better AI features — Azure DevOps or Jira?

As of 2026, Azure DevOps has a significant AI advantage through its native GitHub Copilot integration. Copilot can now operate in agentic mode — turning work items into code changes, creating pull requests, and even debugging issues autonomously. Jira's Atlassian Intelligence offers useful features like natural-language search, AI-powered sprint planning suggestions, and issue summarization through Rovo, but these are assistive rather than agentic. For pure developer productivity, Microsoft's AI capabilities are ahead. For project management intelligence, Atlassian is making strong progress.

### How do I migrate from Azure DevOps to Jira (or vice versa)? [...] ### Azure DevOps + GitHub Copilot

Microsoft's big move in 2026 was bringing agentic AI capabilities to the Azure DevOps workflow through GitHub Copilot. This goes well beyond code completion. Here's what's now available:

 Product Owner creates a User Story in Boards.
 The developer assigns to the Copilot agent; it creates a branch, implements via the MCP context, and links the PR.​
 Pipelines auto-run with IaC suggestions; SRE agent monitors post-deploy.​
 Merge updates to the work item automatically.​

Recognizing the massive installed base of Azure DevOps users—including 90% of the Fortune 100 —Microsoft has introduced a "Hybrid" workflow. This strategy creates a bridge that allows Azure Boards (Project Management) to orchestrate AI agents that operate on GitHub repositories. This is the practical answer for organizations that cannot simply abandon Azure DevOps. 

Supporting Visual 2: Hybrid Workflow Architecture Diagram

The hybrid workflow connecting Azure Boards to GitHub’s server-side AI agents.

### 5.1 The Architecture of Hybrid Intelligence

The integration centers on the Azure Boards + GitHub Copilot connection. This feature allows a Work Item in Azure DevOps (e.g., a User Story or Bug) to serve as the trigger for an AI agent living in GitHub. 

The Workflow: [...] In a traditional workflow, a developer reads a GitHub Issue, mentally formulates a plan, finds the relevant files, and begins typing. Copilot Workspace automates the cognitive "pre-work." Upon opening an issue, the Agentic AI scans the repository's server-side index to understand the current state. It then generates a Specification (a natural language description of the problem and solution) and a Plan (a step-by-step list of files to create, modify, or delete). [...] This workflow effectively positions Azure DevOps as the "Command and Control" layer, while GitHub serves as the "Execution" layer where the AI actually lives and works.

### 5.2 The Azure DevOps MCP Server

To further deepen this connection, Microsoft released the Azure DevOps Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server. MCP is an open standard that enables AI models to interact with external tools and data sources. 

The ADO MCP Server allows GitHub Copilot (running in VS Code or on GitHub.com) to "reach back" into Azure DevOps to fetch context. For example, a developer in VS Code can ask Copilot: "Summarize the acceptance criteria for my active bugs in ADO and generate test cases for them in this GitHub repo."

# How is Azure Document Intelligence priced

![](data:image/svg+xml, %3Csvg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' height='64' class='font-weight-bold' style='font: 600 30.11764705882353px "SegoeUI", Arial' width='64'%3E%3Ccircle fill='hsl(192, 21%, 28%)' cx='32' cy='32' r='32' /%3E%3Ctext x='50%25' y='55%25' dominant-baseline='middle' text-anchor='middle' fill='%23FFF' %3ECH%3C/text%3E%3C/svg%3E)

How is Azure Document Intelligence priced, what are the modules and what is the subscription to process 50,000 pages per year.

An Azure service that turns documents into usable data. Previously known as Azure Form Recognizer.

## 2 answers

![](https://learn.microsoft.com/api/profile-avatar-storage/images/fhe9LaZpV0Go9JtPKHT0YQ.png?8DA448)

Hi Chris,

Azure Document Intelligence uses a pay-as-you-go model based on the number of pages you process. The pricing tiers differ based on the features you need, which is why understanding the modules is key.

The service is structured around two main types of models:

Prebuilt Models: These are ready-to-use for common documents like invoices, receipts, ID cards, and general layouts. You are charged per page.

Custom Models: You can train these on your own document types for higher accuracy. There's a cost for training the model and a separate, usually lower, cost for analyzing pages with it.

For your specific case of 50,000 pages per year, here's my recommendation:

I suggest using the General Document prebuilt model (part of the "Read" and "Layout" functionality). It's a great, cost-effective starting point for most text and structure extraction needs.

At the S0 pricing tier, this model costs $1.25 per 100 pages.

For 50,000 pages, your estimated annual cost would be: (50,000 / 100) \* $1.25 = **$625**.

There is no separate "subscription" fee; you would just pay for what you use, and this usage would be billed monthly. If your documents are more complex (like invoices where you need to extract specific fields like InvoiceTotal), you would use the specialized prebuilt Invoice model, which is priced higher.

If you have a more consistent, predictable monthly usage, you could consider an Azure savings plan for compute to reduce costs, but for your volume, pay-as-you-go is likely the most straightforward.
